lessons.title: Sun, Moon and Stars
objectives: Describe what we see in the sky in the day and at night
Know never to look directly at the Sun
explanation: In the daytime, the Sun shines in the sky. It gives us light and warmth. The Sun is a star — a giant ball of hot glowing gas — the closest star to us.
At night, our side of the Earth turns away from the Sun, so it gets dark. Then we can often see the Moon and many other stars twinkling far away.
Never look straight at the Sun, even with sunglasses — it can hurt your eyes.

lessons.title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
objectives: Name full moon, half moon and crescent moon
Notice the Moon's shape changes over a month
prerequisites: Knows we see the Moon at night
explanation: The Moon looks like a different shape on different nights. Sometimes it is a full, round circle (full moon). Sometimes it is half. Sometimes it is a thin curve called a crescent.
The Moon doesn't really change shape. It is always a round ball. The Sun lights up half of it, and we see different amounts of the lit half as the Moon travels around the Earth.
It takes about a month for the Moon to go from new moon to full moon and back again. Many festivals, like Eid and Diwali, are timed by the Moon.

objectives: Explain day and night using Earth's rotation

prerequisites: Knows the Sun lights the day
explanation: The Earth is a giant ball that spins like a top. One complete spin takes about 24 hours — one day.
The side facing the Sun has daytime; the side facing away has night. The Sun seems to move across the sky, but really it is the Earth turning.
While spinning, the Earth also travels around the Sun in a big path called an orbit. One full orbit takes about 365 days — one year.

lessons.title: Meet the Planets
objectives: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun
Describe one feature of each planet
explanation: Eight planets orbit our Sun. In order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. A memory trick: "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming."
The first four are small and rocky. Mars is red because of rusty dust. Venus is the hottest planet because its thick clouds trap heat.
The outer four are giants made mostly of gas or ice. Jupiter is the biggest; Saturn has beautiful rings. Pluto used to be called a planet but is now classed as a dwarf planet.

context.text: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined "planet" in a way that reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet.

lessons.title: Star Patterns
objectives: Identify a constellation and explain what it is
Distinguish astronomy from astrology
prerequisites: Knows stars are like the Sun
explanation: Stars are suns, but so far away they look like tiny dots. A constellation is a group of stars that people imagined into a picture. The stars in a constellation may be very different distances from us.

Orion the Hunter has three bright stars in a row for his belt. The Big Dipper (part of Ursa Major) is known in India as the Saptarishi — the seven sages. Different cultures saw different pictures in the same stars.

Astronomy is the science of space, based on observation and evidence. Astrology is a traditional belief that star and planet positions influence people's lives; scientific tests have not found evidence that it predicts personality or events.

context.text: In Indian tradition, the seven bright stars of the Big Dipper are named after the Saptarishi, the seven sages, and the star Polaris is associated with Dhruva.
Controlled studies have not found that astrological predictions perform better than chance.

vocabulary.meaning: a named pattern of stars

examples: Orion is easy to see in winter evenings.

lessons.title: A Day as an Astronaut
objectives: Describe how astronauts live in microgravity
Name Indian contributions to human spaceflight
explanation: Rockets push hot gas downward very fast, which pushes the rocket up. To get into orbit, a spacecraft must reach about 28,000 km/h.

On the International Space Station, astronauts float because they and the station are falling around the Earth together — this is called microgravity. They sleep in sleeping bags tied to walls, exercise daily to keep bones and muscles strong, and drink from pouches.

Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian citizen in space in 1984, aboard a Soviet mission. Kalpana Chawla, born in India, flew on NASA Space Shuttle missions. India's Gaganyaan programme is preparing Indian astronauts to launch on an Indian rocket.

context.text: Rakesh Sharma flew aboard Soyuz T-11 in April 1984. Kalpana Chawla flew on STS-87 (1997) and died in the Columbia accident in 2003.

lessons.title: Eclipses
objectives: Explain solar and lunar eclipses with a model
Explain why seasons happen
prerequisites: Knows rotation, orbit and Moon phases
explanation: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking the Sun's light for some places. Never look at a solar eclipse without proper eclipse glasses — it can permanently damage eyes.
A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth passes between the Sun and Moon, so Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. The Moon can look red. It is safe to watch.

Seasons happen because Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. When our hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, sunlight is more direct and days are longer — summer. It is not because Earth is closer to the Sun.

context.text: Many cultures told stories to explain eclipses; in Indian tradition, Rahu and Ketu are said to swallow the Sun or Moon.
Indian astronomer Āryabhaṭa (5th century CE) explained eclipses as shadows cast by the Earth and Moon.

story.title: Āryabhaṭa's Shadows

lessons.title: ISRO's Great Missions
objectives: Describe major ISRO missions and their achievements
Explain why space missions matter on Earth
explanation: The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched India's first satellite, Aryabhata, in 1975 (on a Soviet rocket). Today ISRO builds rockets like the PSLV and LVM3.

Chandrayaan-1 (2008) helped detect water molecules on the Moon. Mangalyaan, the Mars Orbiter Mission, reached Mars orbit in 2014 on its first attempt. Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole region in August 2023, making India the first country to land there.
Aditya-L1, launched in 2023, studies the Sun from a point about 1.5 million km from Earth. Satellites also help us every day with weather forecasts, maps, communication and disaster warnings.

context.text: Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander touched down on 23 August 2023; India now celebrates 23 August as National Space Day.

lessons.title: How Stars Live and Die
objectives: Describe the main stages in a star's life
Explain how stars produce energy by fusion
prerequisites: Knows the Sun is a star
explanation: Stars form in nebulae — huge clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls the material together until the centre gets hot enough for nuclear fusion: hydrogen nuclei join to make helium, releasing enormous energy.
A star like the Sun shines steadily for about 10 billion years, then swells into a red giant, and finally becomes a small, dense white dwarf.

Much more massive stars burn faster and end in a huge explosion called a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole. Supernovae spread elements like iron and gold into space — the atoms in your body were made in stars.

context.text: The Indian-American astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar calculated the maximum mass of a white dwarf (about 1.4 solar masses), the "Chandrasekhar limit", and shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.

lessons.title: How Big Is Space?
objectives: Explain what a light-year is
Describe our place in the Milky Way galaxy
prerequisites: Knows the speed of light is very fast
explanation: Light travels about 300,000 km every second. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year — about 9.5 trillion kilometres. It is a unit of distance, not time.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us. The nearest star beyond the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away — so we see it as it was over four years ago.
Our Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across. The observable universe contains billions of galaxies.

lessons.title: The Big Bang: Evidence
objectives: Explain the main evidence for the Big Bang model
Distinguish scientific cosmology from religious and philosophical accounts
explanation: In the 1920s, Edwin Hubble found that distant galaxies' light is redshifted — stretched to longer wavelengths — and that farther galaxies recede faster. The universe is expanding.

Running the expansion backward suggests the universe was once extremely hot and dense, about 13.8 billion years ago. This is the Big Bang model — not an explosion in space, but the expansion of space itself.

In 1965, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation was discovered: faint leftover heat from the early universe, strong evidence for the model. Science describes how the universe evolved; questions of why there is a universe at all are explored by philosophy and religious traditions in their own ways.

context.text: Georges Lemaître proposed an expanding universe from a "primeval atom" in 1927; current measurements give an age of about 13.8 billion years.

Many religious traditions have creation accounts; Hindu cosmology, for example, describes vast repeating cycles of creation and dissolution. Followers interpret these in various ways, and many see no conflict with scientific cosmology.

vocabulary.meaning: stretching of light from objects moving away
radiation left over from the early universe
the study of the universe's origin and evolution
the growth of space over time

examples: A raisin loaf rising: every raisin moves away from every other.

story.title: The Pigeon Problem
story.text: In 1965, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found a faint, steady hiss in their radio antenna that came from every direction. They even cleaned out pigeon droppings, thinking that was the cause! The hiss remained. It turned out to be the cosmic microwave background — the afterglow of the early universe.

Explain how exoplanets are detected and what makes a world habitable
explanation: Many cultures advanced astronomy. Babylonians recorded planetary positions; Greek astronomers measured Earth's size; Indian astronomers like Āryabhaṭa proposed Earth's rotation; scholars in the Islamic world refined observations and instruments; Chinese astronomers recorded supernovae; the Maya built precise calendars. Copernicus (1543) and Galileo's telescope observations (1610) supported a Sun-centred system.
Since 1995, astronomers have confirmed thousands of exoplanets — planets around other stars — mostly by detecting a star's dimming as a planet passes in front (transit method) or a star's wobble.

A "habitable zone" is the region around a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface. Astrobiologists also look for biosignatures — gases in atmospheres that might indicate life. So far, no life beyond Earth has been confirmed.

context.text: In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz detected 51 Pegasi b, the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star, earning a share of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. Jantar Mantar observatories built by Sawai Jai Singh II in the 18th century still stand in Jaipur and Delhi.

story.title: The Dimming Star
story.text: A student analysing public telescope data noticed a star dimming slightly every 12 days, then brightening again. The dips were identical each time. "Something is passing in front of it," she realised. Professional astronomers confirmed it: a new exoplanet, found by careful attention to tiny changes.
